title: Renaissance art and linear perspective
examples: How did Renaissance artists make paintings look three-dimensional?
What is the relationship between humanism and Renaissance art?
Who paid for the art during the Renaissance?

explain.say: Today we learn about Renaissance art techniques. We will look at how artists created depth. First we study the vanishing point.
The vanishing point is the spot on the horizon line. All parallel lines appear to meet there. Think of train tracks going far away.

items: Vanishing point is on horizon line
Parallel lines appear to meet there

explain.say: Next we explore humanism in art. This idea focused on human potential and worth. People became the center of study again.
Patrons were people who paid for art. They were wealthy individuals or families. They supported artists' work greatly.
In real life, think about a long hallway in a museum. The floor tiles seem to meet at one point. That point is the vanishing point.

items: Tiles appear to meet at one point
This point is the vanishing point

explain.say: A common mistake is forgetting the horizon line. You must place your vanishing point on the correct line. This keeps the perspective accurate.

faq.q: What is the difference between perspective and depth?
faq.a: Perspective is the technique artists use to create the illusion of depth. It mathematically shows how objects get smaller further away.
asks: Is perspective the same as depth?

faq.q: Did humanism mean art was only about people?
faq.a: No, it meant that human life and achievements were worthy of study. Artists celebrated human potential alongside religious themes.
asks: Was humanism a rejection of religion?
What did humanism emphasize in art?

faq.a: Patrons could be wealthy families, powerful guilds, or even the Church itself. They commissioned works to show their status and piety.
asks: Did the Church act as a patron?

faq.q: How does the vanishing point work with different objects?
faq.a: The vanishing point is used for any set of parallel lines receding into space. It is not limited to roads or tracks.
asks: Do I use one vanishing point for everything?
Can I use multiple vanishing points?

faq.q: If I use humanism, do I have to paint people?
faq.a: No, you can show humanism through themes of classical learning or scientific observation. It is more about the focus of the art.
asks: What is the core idea of humanism?

facts: Linear perspective uses geometry to create depth on a flat surface.
Humanism shifted focus from purely divine matters to human experience.
Patrons provided the financial support that allowed major art projects to happen.
The vanishing point is the single point where receding parallel lines appear to meet.

quiz.say: If you draw a long row of square columns receding into the distance, where must all the vertical lines appear to meet?

options.show: The bottom edge of the picture
options.say: The bottom edge of the picture

quiz.why: The vanishing point is the specific location where all parallel lines in one set appear to converge.

wrong.1: The center is only correct if the lines are perfectly symmetrical, but not always.
wrong.2: The bottom edge is where the viewer stands, not where the lines meet.
wrong.3: The horizon line is the level of the vanishing point, but not the point itself.

quiz.say: The Renaissance idea that celebrated human potential is called:
quiz.why: Humanism placed value on human reason and achievement, marking a shift in intellectual focus.

wrong.0: Humanity is a general concept, while Humanism is the specific intellectual movement.
wrong.1: Classicism refers to style, but Humanism is the underlying philosophical driver.
wrong.3: Naturalism is about realistic depiction, not the core philosophy.

quiz.say: Who were the people who funded and commissioned Renaissance artworks?
quiz.why: Patrons were the wealthy sponsors who provided the necessary money for artists to work.

wrong.0: Guilds were groups of workers, but patrons were the financial backers.
wrong.1: While the Church was a major patron, it was not the only source of funding.
wrong.3: Artists were the ones creating the work, not paying for it.
